source: Steele, Bhattacharya et al. (Cornell University, with University of Nebraska-Lincoln, UT Austin, University at Buffalo, Clark Atlanta University and Lund University), 'A 7-eV bandgap semiconductor based on silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3', Nature, published 7 October 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-11085-3. Devices named AlphaDiode and AlphaFET. Not stored or shown.
title: A 7-electronvolt oxide semiconductor that works as a diode and transistor
description: A thin crystal film of aluminium gallium oxide, grown layer by layer on a cheap sapphire wafer and seeded with silicon atoms, has a bandgap above 7 electronvolts yet still carries current. The bandgap is the energy an electron needs to break free; a wider one lets a power switch block more voltage in a thinner layer. A diode and a transistor have been built from the film.
body:
Power converters in chargers and grid equipment waste less energy and get smaller when their switches use materials with wider bandgaps. A standard measure of how good such a switch can be grows with the bandgap raised to the power 5.5. The catch is that the wider the bandgap, the harder it is to add impurity atoms that make the material conduct. This film breaks that pattern: above 6 electronvolts it conducts more than 100 million times better than any earlier report, and its bandgap is wider than that of cubic boron nitride, the next-widest known semiconductor.

The base it grows on matters as much as the film. Sapphire is cheap, comes in large, high-quality crystals, and is already made at massive scale. Diamond and cubic boron nitride, the usual very-wide-bandgap candidates, need high-pressure synthesis and come only as small, costly samples.

The first devices are proofs of concept, not products. Electrons move slowly through the film, the silicon atoms hold on to their electrons tightly so only some are freed at room temperature, and the matching p-type version of the material, which many devices need, has not been made yet.
